subsections.title: The Parts of an Air Brake System

facts.text: Air brakes are three braking systems in one: the service brake, the parking brake, and the emergency brake.
The service brake system puts on and releases the brakes when you use the brake pedal in normal driving.
The parking brake system puts on and releases the parking brakes when you use the parking brake control.
The emergency brake system uses parts of the service and parking brake systems to stop the vehicle if the brake system fails.

cards.q: What three braking systems make up air brakes?
cards.a: Service brake, parking brake and emergency brake.

cards.q: What does the emergency brake system use?
cards.a: Parts of the service and parking brake systems.

exam.q: Air brakes are really how many braking systems?
exam.why: Service, parking and emergency brakes together make the air brake system.

reading.p: Air brakes use compressed air to stop the vehicle. They stop large, heavy vehicles well, but only if they are kept in good order and used correctly.
What people call air brakes is really three braking systems that share the same parts.

ul: The service brake system puts the brakes on and lets them off when you use the brake pedal in normal driving.
The parking brake system puts the parking brakes on and lets them off when you use the parking brake control.
The emergency brake system uses parts of the other two to stop the vehicle if the brake system fails.

reading.note: Learn these three by name. The test asks for them.

facts.text: The air compressor pumps air into the air storage tanks, and it is driven by the engine through gears or a v-belt.
If the air compressor has its own oil supply, check the oil level before you drive.

cards.q: What does the air compressor do?
cards.a: It pumps air into the air storage tanks.

cards.q: What must you check if the compressor has its own oil supply?
cards.a: The oil level, before driving.

reading.p: The air compressor pumps air into the air storage tanks. The engine drives it, through gears or a v-belt.

ul: It may be cooled by air, or by the engine cooling system.
It may have its own oil supply, or it may use the engine oil.

reading.note: If the compressor has its own oil supply, check the oil level before you drive.

facts.text: The governor stops the compressor pumping at the cut-out level, which is about 125 psi.
The governor lets the compressor start pumping again at the cut-in level, which is about 100 psi.

cards.q: At what pressure does the governor cut out?
cards.a: About 125 psi.

cards.q: At what pressure does the governor cut in?
cards.a: About 100 psi.

cards.q: What does the air compressor governor control?
cards.a: When the compressor pumps air into the tanks.

exam.q: At about what pressure does the governor stop the compressor pumping?
exam.why: Cut-out is about 125 psi. Cut-in is about 100 psi.

exam.q: At about what pressure does the compressor start pumping again?
exam.why: Cut-in is about 100 psi.

reading.p: The governor decides when the compressor pumps. It does not make the air. It only switches the pumping on and off, to hold the tank pressure in a band.

numbers.what: cut-out: the governor stops the pumping
cut-in: the governor starts the pumping again

reading.note: These two numbers come up again in the final brake check in step 7. Learn them now.

facts.text: The air tanks hold enough compressed air to use the brakes several times, even after the compressor stops working.

cards.q: How much air do the tanks hold?
cards.a: Enough to use the brakes several times, even if the compressor stops.

reading.p: The air storage tanks hold the compressed air. The number of tanks and their size change from vehicle to vehicle.

reading.note: The tanks hold enough air to use the brakes several times, even after the compressor stops working.

facts.text: Compressed air holds water and compressor oil, and the water can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure.
With manual drain valves you must drain the tanks yourself at the end of each day of driving.
A manual drain valve is worked by a quarter turn or by pulling a cable, and an automatic valve forces the water and oil out by itself.

cards.q: Why must air tanks be drained?
cards.a: Water and oil collect in them, and water can freeze and cause brake failure.

cards.q: How often do you drain manual air tanks?
cards.a: At the end of each day of driving.

exam.q: Why must you drain the air tanks?
exam.why: Water and compressor oil collect in the tanks, and water can freeze and stop the brakes working.

reading.p: Compressed air carries water and a little compressor oil. Both are bad for the brakes. In cold weather the water can freeze, and then the brakes fail.
The water and the oil settle in the bottom of the tank, where a drain valve lets them out. There are two kinds.

ul: Manual: you turn it a quarter turn or pull a cable. You must drain the tanks yourself at the end of each day of driving.
Automatic: it pushes the water and oil out by itself. It may also have a manual drain.

reading.p: An automatic tank can have an electric heater, which stops the drain freezing in cold weather.

reading.note: Drain the tanks completely. A tank you drain halfway still holds water.

facts.text: An alcohol evaporator puts alcohol into the air system to cut the risk of ice in the air brake valves in cold weather.
Check the alcohol container and fill it as needed every day in cold weather, and still drain the tanks daily.

cards.q: What does an alcohol evaporator do?
cards.a: It puts alcohol in the air system to stop ice forming in the valves.

reading.p: Some air brake systems have an alcohol evaporator. It puts alcohol into the air system, which cuts the risk of ice in the brake valves and the other parts in cold weather. Ice inside the system stops the brakes working.

reading.note: In cold weather, check the alcohol container every day and fill it as needed. You must still drain the tanks daily.

facts.text: The safety relief valve is in the first tank the compressor pumps to, and it is usually set to open at 150 psi.
If the safety valve lets air out, something is wrong, and a mechanic must fix it.

cards.q: At what pressure does the safety valve usually open?
cards.a: 150 psi.

cards.q: Where is the safety relief valve fitted?
cards.a: In the first tank the compressor pumps air to.

cards.q: What does it mean if the safety valve releases air?
cards.a: Something is wrong. Have a mechanic fix it.

exam.q: The safety relief valve is usually set to open at what pressure?
exam.why: The safety valve usually opens at 150 psi.

reading.p: The safety relief valve protects the tanks and the rest of the system from too much pressure. It sits in the first tank the compressor pumps to.

numbers.what: the pressure at which the safety valve usually opens

reading.note: If the safety valve lets air out, something is wrong. Have a mechanic find the fault and fix it.

facts.text: Pushing the brake pedal harder applies more air pressure, and letting it up releases the brakes and lets air out of the system.
Pressing and releasing the pedal when you do not need to lets air out faster than the compressor can replace it, and the brakes stop working if the pressure gets too low.

cards.q: What is the danger of fanning the brake pedal?
cards.a: Air goes out faster than the compressor replaces it, and the brakes fail at low pressure.

cards.q: What else is the brake pedal called?
cards.a: The foot valve or treadle valve.

reading.p: You put the brakes on with the brake pedal, which is also called the foot valve or the treadle valve.

ul: Push the pedal down harder and more air pressure goes to the brakes.
Let the pedal up and the pressure drops and the brakes come off.

reading.p: Each time you let the brakes off, some air leaves the system, and the compressor must replace it.

reading.note: Do not fan the pedal. Pressing and releasing it when you do not need to lets air out faster than the compressor can replace it, and the brakes stop working when the pressure gets too low.

facts.text: The most common foundation brake is the s-cam drum brake.
To stop, the brake shoes and linings are pushed against the inside of the drum, which makes friction and heat, and too much heat makes the brakes stop working.
Wedge brakes and disc brakes are less common than s-cam brakes.

cards.q: What is the most common type of foundation brake?
cards.a: The s-cam drum brake.

cards.q: What slows the vehicle inside a drum brake?
cards.a: Friction, as the shoes and linings press the inside of the drum.

reading.p: Foundation brakes are the brakes at each wheel. The most common kind is the s-cam drum brake.

A brake drum sits at each end of an axle, and the wheel bolts to the drum. The braking parts are inside. To stop, the brake shoes and linings press the inside of the drum. That makes friction, which slows the vehicle and makes heat. Too much heat stops the brakes working.

ul: You push the brake pedal, and air goes into the brake chamber.
The air pushes the rod out, which moves the slack adjuster.
The slack adjuster twists the brake camshaft, which turns the s-cam.
The s-cam forces the shoes apart, against the inside of the drum.
You let the pedal up, the s-cam turns back, and a spring pulls the shoes off the drum.

reading.p: Wedge brakes push a wedge between the ends of two shoes. Disc brakes use a power screw to clamp the disc between pads, like a large c-clamp. Both are less common than s-cam brakes.

facts.text: Every vehicle with air brakes has a supply pressure gauge that shows how much pressure is in the air tanks, and a dual system has one for each half, or one gauge with two needles.

cards.q: What does the supply pressure gauge show?
cards.a: How much pressure is in the air tanks.

reading.p: The supply pressure gauge tells you how much pressure is in the air tanks. Every vehicle with air brakes has one.

reading.note: A dual air brake system has a gauge for each half of the system, or one gauge with two needles.

facts.text: The application pressure gauge shows how much air pressure you are putting on the brakes.
If you need more and more application pressure to hold the same speed, the brakes are fading, so slow down and take a lower gear.

cards.q: What does rising application pressure at the same speed mean?
cards.a: The brakes are fading. Slow down and use a lower gear.

exam.q: You need more application pressure to hold your speed. What does this mean?
exam.why: More pressure for the same speed means fading brakes, brakes out of adjustment, leaks or a mechanical fault.

reading.p: The application pressure gauge shows how much air pressure you are putting on the brakes. Not every vehicle has one.

reading.note: If you need more and more pressure to hold the same speed, the brakes are fading. Slow down and take a lower gear.

reading.p: Brakes out of adjustment, air leaks or a mechanical fault can also make you need more pressure.

facts.text: A low air pressure warning you can see must come on before the tank pressure falls below 55 psi.
A low air pressure warning signal is required on every vehicle with air brakes, and it is usually a red light, sometimes with a buzzer.
A wig wag drops a mechanical arm into view when the pressure falls below 55 psi, and an automatic one rises out of view only above 55 psi.
On large buses the low pressure warning often comes on at 80 to 85 psi.

cards.q: Before what pressure must the low air warning come on?
cards.a: Before the pressure falls below 55 psi.

cards.q: Is a low air pressure warning required?
cards.a: Yes, on every vehicle with air brakes.

cards.q: What is a wig wag?
cards.a: A mechanical arm that drops into view when pressure falls below 55 psi.

cards.q: At what pressure do large buses usually warn of low air?
cards.a: 80 to 85 psi.

exam.q: The low air pressure warning must come on before the pressure drops below what?
exam.why: The visible warning must come on before 55 psi.

reading.p: Every vehicle with air brakes must have a low air pressure warning signal. It is usually a red light, and a buzzer may sound with it.

numbers.what: the warning must come on BEFORE the pressure falls below this
where a large bus often warns instead

reading.p: A wig wag is another kind of warning. It drops a mechanical arm into your view when the pressure falls below 55 psi.

ul: An automatic wig wag rises out of view by itself, but only once the pressure is above 55 psi.
A manual wig wag must be pushed out of view by hand, and it will not stay up until the pressure is above 55 psi.

facts.text: The stop light switch is an electric switch worked by air pressure, and it turns on your brake lights when you put on the air brakes.

cards.q: What does the stop light switch do?
cards.a: It turns on the brake lights when you apply the air brakes.

reading.p: Drivers behind you must know when you brake. The stop light switch is an electric switch worked by air pressure, and it turns on your brake lights when you put the air brakes on.

facts.text: A front brake limiting valve, on some vehicles made before 1975, cuts the normal air pressure to the front brakes by half when the cab control is set to slippery.
Front wheel braking is good in all conditions, and tests show a front wheel skid from braking is not likely even on ice, so keep the control in the normal position.
An automatic front wheel limiting valve cuts the air to the front brakes except in a very hard application of 55 psi or more, and the driver cannot control it.

cards.q: Are front wheel brakes good on slippery roads?
cards.a: Yes. Front wheel braking is good in all conditions.

cards.q: What does the slippery setting of a front brake limiting valve do?
cards.a: It halves the air pressure to the front brakes, and cuts your stopping power.

exam.q: Front wheel brakes on a slippery road are:
exam.why: Front wheel braking is good in all conditions, and a braking skid at the front is unlikely even on ice.

reading.p: Some vehicles made before 1975 have a front brake limiting valve, with a control in the cab marked normal and slippery.
In the slippery position the valve cuts the normal air pressure to the front brakes by half. The idea was to stop the front wheels skidding.

reading.note: It does not help. It only cuts your stopping power. Front wheel braking is good in all conditions, and tests show a front wheel braking skid is unlikely even on ice. Keep the control in the normal position.

reading.p: Many vehicles have an automatic front wheel limiting valve instead. It cuts the air to the front brakes except in a very hard application of 55 psi or more, and the driver cannot control it.

facts.text: Every truck, truck tractor and bus must have emergency brakes and parking brakes held on by mechanical force, because air pressure leaks away, and spring brakes do that job.
When you drive, air pressure holds the powerful springs back. Take the air away and the springs put the brakes on.
Tractor and straight truck spring brakes come fully on when the air pressure drops to between 20 and 45 psi, and typically 20 to 30 psi.
Do not wait for the spring brakes to come on by themselves. Stop safely as soon as the low air warning comes on, while you still control the brakes.
Spring brake power depends on the brakes being in adjustment, because badly adjusted brakes make the regular, emergency and parking brakes all work poorly.

cards.q: What are spring brakes?
cards.a: Brakes held off by air pressure. If the air goes, the springs apply them.

cards.q: At what pressure do spring brakes come fully on?
cards.a: Between 20 and 45 psi, typically 20 to 30 psi.

cards.q: What do you do when the low air warning comes on?
cards.a: Stop safely right away, while you can still control the brakes.

exam.q: At what pressure do tractor and straight truck spring brakes come fully on?
exam.why: They come fully on between 20 and 45 psi, typically 20 to 30.

exam.q: The low air pressure warning comes on while you drive. What should you do?
choices: Keep going to the next stop
Pump the brake pedal to build air
exam.why: Stop while you still have enough air to control the brakes. Do not wait for the spring brakes.

reading.p: Every truck, truck tractor and bus must have emergency brakes and parking brakes that are held on by mechanical force, because air pressure leaks away in time. Spring brakes do that job.

ul: While you drive, air pressure holds powerful springs back.
Take the air away and the springs put the brakes on.
The parking brake control lets the air out of the spring brakes, so the springs apply them.
A leak that loses all the air will also let the springs put the brakes on.

numbers.what: where tractor and straight truck spring brakes come fully on, typically 20 to 30

reading.note: Do not wait for the spring brakes to come on by themselves. Stop safely as soon as the low air warning shows, while you still control the brakes.

reading.p: Spring brake power depends on the brakes being in adjustment. Badly adjusted brakes make the service brakes and the emergency and parking brakes all work poorly.

facts.text: On a newer vehicle the parking brake control is a yellow, diamond-shaped push-pull knob. Pull it out to put the parking brakes on, and push it in to release them.
Never push the brake pedal down while the spring brakes are on, because the springs and the air pressure together can damage the brakes.
A modulating control valve puts the spring brakes on gradually, so you can control them if the service brakes fail.
A separate air tank with dual parking control valves can release the spring brakes to move the vehicle in an emergency, and it holds only enough air for a few moves.

cards.q: What does the parking brake control look like on a newer vehicle?
cards.a: A yellow, diamond-shaped push-pull knob.

cards.q: Why must you not press the brake pedal with the spring brakes on?
cards.a: The springs and the air pressure together can damage the brakes.

exam.q: What shape and colour is the parking brake control on a newer vehicle?
exam.why: It is a yellow, diamond-shaped push-pull knob. Older vehicles may have a round blue knob or a lever.

reading.p: On a newer vehicle the parking brake control is a yellow, diamond-shaped push-pull knob. Pull it out to put the parking brakes on. Push it in to let them off. An older vehicle may use a lever.

reading.note: Never push the brake pedal down while the spring brakes are on. The springs and the air pressure together can damage the brakes. Some systems are built to prevent this, but not all, and those that are do not always work.

reading.h: Two other controls you may meet

ul: A modulating control valve puts the spring brakes on gradually, so you can still control the vehicle if the service brakes fail. To park, move the lever as far as it goes and lock it.
Dual parking control valves use a separate air tank to let the spring brakes off, so you can move the vehicle in an emergency. The tank holds enough air for only a few moves, so plan before you move.

facts.text: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after 1 March 1997 must have antilock brakes.
Other air brake vehicles, which are trucks, buses, trailers and converter dollies, must have antilock brakes if they were built on or after 1 March 1998.
Check the certification label for the date of manufacture to find out whether your vehicle has ABS.
ABS malfunction lamps are yellow. A tractor, truck or bus has it on the instrument panel, and a trailer has it on the left side, at the front or the rear corner.
The malfunction lamp comes on at start-up for a bulb check and then goes out. On an older system it may stay on until you are driving over five mph.
ABS is an addition to your normal brakes. It does not decrease or increase your normal braking, and it works only when the wheels are about to lock.
ABS does not always shorten your stopping distance, but it helps you keep control in hard braking.
To find ABS on an older towed unit, look under the vehicle for the electronic control unit and the wheel speed sensor wires at the back of the brakes.

cards.q: Which air brake tractors must have ABS?
cards.a: Truck tractors built on or after 1 March 1997.

cards.q: Which other air brake vehicles must have ABS?
cards.a: Trucks, buses, trailers and converter dollies built on or after 1 March 1998.

cards.q: What colour is the ABS malfunction lamp?
cards.a: Yellow.

cards.q: Where is a trailer's ABS malfunction lamp?
cards.a: On the left side, at the front or rear corner.

cards.q: Does ABS shorten your stopping distance?
cards.a: Not necessarily. It helps you stay in control during hard braking.

cards.q: How do you tell whether your vehicle has ABS?
cards.a: Check the certification label for the date of manufacture.

exam.q: From which date must a truck tractor with air brakes have antilock brakes?
exam.why: Tractors from 1 March 1997, and other air brake vehicles from 1 March 1998.

exam.q: What does ABS do for your braking?
choices: It keeps the wheels from locking so you stay in control
exam.why: ABS only works when a wheel is about to lock. It does not necessarily shorten the stop.

reading.p: An antilock braking system is a computer that stops your wheels locking up in hard braking.

numbers.what: truck tractors with air brakes built on or after this date
other air brake vehicles: trucks, buses, trailers and converter dollies

reading.p: Many vehicles built before those dates were given ABS anyway. Check the certification label for the date of manufacture.

ul: The lamp is yellow.
On a tractor, a truck or a bus it is on the instrument panel.
On a trailer it is on the left side, at the front or the rear corner.
It comes on at start-up for a bulb check and then goes out. On an older system it may stay on until you are driving over five mph.
If it stays on after the bulb check, or comes on while you drive, you may have lost ABS at one or more wheels.

reading.note: ABS is an addition to your normal brakes. It does not increase or decrease your normal braking, and it works only when a wheel is about to lock. It does not always shorten your stopping distance, but it helps you keep control.

reading.p: On an older towed unit, look under the vehicle for the electronic control unit and the wheel speed sensor wires at the back of the brakes.

facts.text: A dual air brake system is two separate air brake systems that share one set of brake controls, and each has its own tanks, hoses and lines.
One system works the rear axle brakes and the other works the front axle brakes, and both feed air to the trailer. The first is the primary system and the other is the secondary system.
Before you drive a vehicle with a dual air system, let the compressor build at least 100 psi in both the primary and the secondary system.
The warning light and buzzer must go off above 55 psi, and must come on before the pressure falls below 55 psi in either system.
If one air system gets very low, the front or the rear brakes will not work fully, so it takes longer to stop. Park safely and have the system fixed.

cards.q: What is a dual air brake system?
cards.a: Two separate air brake systems with one set of controls, each with its own tanks and lines.

cards.q: How much pressure must be in both systems before driving?
cards.a: At least 100 psi.

cards.q: What happens if one system of a dual air brake system goes very low?
cards.a: The front or rear brakes stop working fully, so stopping takes longer.

exam.q: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air brake system, what pressure must you have?
choices: At least 55 psi in one system
At least 100 psi in both systems
At least 125 psi in one system
At least 150 psi in both systems
exam.why: Let the compressor build a minimum of 100 psi in both the primary and secondary systems.

reading.p: Most heavy vehicles have a dual air brake system, for safety. It is two separate air brake systems that share one set of brake controls, and each one has its own tanks, hoses and lines.

ul: The primary system usually works the brakes on the rear axle or axles.
The secondary system works the brakes on the front axle, and perhaps one rear axle.
Both systems feed air to the trailer, if there is one.

numbers.what: the least pressure to build in BOTH systems before you move
the warning light and buzzer must come on before either system falls below this

reading.p: Watch both gauges, or both needles in the one gauge. The warning should shut off as the pressure rises past the value the maker sets, which must be above 55 psi.

reading.note: If one system gets very low, the front or the rear brakes stop working fully, so it takes you longer to stop. Park safely and have the system fixed.

facts.text: Inspect a vehicle with air brakes with the same seven-step method as any other vehicle, and add the air brake checks in the step where each one belongs.

cards.q: Which inspection method covers air brakes?
cards.a: The same seven-step method, with extra air brake checks added in.

reading.p: Inspect a vehicle with air brakes with the same seven-step method as any other vehicle. There are simply more things to check, and each one belongs in a particular step.

ul: Step 2, the engine compartment: the compressor drive belt.
Step 5, the walk-around: slack adjusters, drums, linings and hoses.
Step 7, instead of the hydraulic brake check: the full air brake check.

facts.text: In step 2, the engine compartment check, look at the condition and the tightness of the air compressor drive belt if the compressor is belt-driven.

cards.q: What air brake item do you check in the engine compartment?
cards.a: The air compressor drive belt, if it is belt-driven: condition and tightness.

reading.p: If the air compressor is belt-driven, check the condition and the tightness of the drive belt. It should be in good condition.

facts.text: To check a slack adjuster, park on level ground, chock the wheels, release the parking brakes, put gloves on, and pull hard on each slack adjuster you can reach.
A slack adjuster that moves more than about one inch where the push rod attaches to it probably needs adjustment.
Brakes out of adjustment are the most common fault found in roadside inspections.
Every vehicle built since 1994 has automatic slack adjusters, and they must still be checked.
A brake drum or disc must not have a crack longer than one half the width of the friction area.
Linings must not be loose, soaked with oil or grease, or dangerously thin, and the air hoses to the brake chambers must not be cut or worn.
Adjusting an automatic slack adjuster by hand hides a mechanical fault instead of fixing it, so take the vehicle to a repair shop.

cards.q: How much slack adjuster movement means adjustment is needed?
cards.a: More than about one inch where the push rod attaches.

cards.q: How do you check slack adjusters safely?
cards.a: Park level, chock the wheels, release the parking brakes, wear gloves and pull hard on each one.

cards.q: What is the most common fault found in roadside inspections?
cards.a: Brakes out of adjustment.

cards.q: How long a crack is allowed in a brake drum?
cards.a: No longer than half the width of the friction area.

cards.q: Do automatic slack adjusters still need checking?
cards.a: Yes. Every vehicle since 1994 has them, and they must still be checked.

exam.q: A slack adjuster moves about two inches when you pull hard on it. What does this mean?
choices: It means the spring brakes are on
exam.why: More than about one inch of movement at the push rod means it probably needs adjustment.

exam.q: Before you pull on a slack adjuster you must:
choices: Chock the wheels and release the parking brakes
exam.why: Park level, chock the wheels and release the parking brakes so the slack adjuster can move.

ul: Park on level ground.
Chock the wheels, so the vehicle cannot move.
Release the parking brakes, so the slack adjusters can move.
Put gloves on, and pull hard on each slack adjuster you can reach.

numbers.what: more movement than this, where the push rod attaches, means it probably needs adjustment

reading.note: Brakes out of adjustment are the most common fault found in roadside inspections. A vehicle with too much brake slack can be very hard to stop.

reading.p: Every vehicle built since 1994 has automatic slack adjusters. They adjust themselves in a full brake application, but they must still be checked. Adjusting one by hand usually hides a mechanical fault instead of fixing it, so take the vehicle to a repair shop.

ul: A drum or disc must not have a crack longer than one half the width of the friction area.
Linings must not be loose, soaked with oil or grease, or dangerously thin.
Mechanical parts must be in place, not broken and not missing.
The air hoses to the brake chambers must not be cut or worn from rubbing.

facts.text: Governor check: pumping should start at about 100 psi and stop at about 125 psi.

Leakage test with the brakes released: with a fully charged system, the engine off and the parking brake released, the loss must be less than 2 psi in one minute for a single vehicle and less than 3 psi in one minute for a combination vehicle.
Leakage test with the foot brake fully applied for one minute: more than 3 psi in a minute for a single vehicle, or more than 4 psi for a combination vehicle, is too much.
A fully charged air system is typically 125 psi, and governor cutoff is in the range 120 to 140 psi.
Low pressure warning test: with the engine off and the electrical power on, step on and off the brake pedal. The warning must come on before the pressure falls below 55 psi.
Spring brake test: keep fanning off air, and the parking brake valve, with the tractor protection valve on a tractor-trailer, must pop out between 20 and 45 psi, which puts the spring brakes on.
Pressure buildup in a dual air system must go from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds at operating rpm.
In a single air system made before 1975, pressure must build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes with the engine idling at 600 to 900 rpm.
Parking brake test: stop, put the parking brake on, and pull gently against it in a low gear to check that it holds.
Service brake test: at normal pressure, with the parking brake released, roll forward at about five mph and apply the brakes firmly. Note any pull to one side, an odd feel, or a slow stop.

cards.q: Maximum air loss in one minute with the brakes released?
cards.a: Less than 2 psi for a single vehicle, less than 3 psi for a combination.

cards.q: Maximum air loss in one minute with the foot brake applied?
cards.a: 3 psi for a single vehicle, 4 psi for a combination.

cards.q: How do you test the low pressure warning signal?
cards.a: Engine off, power on, fan the brake pedal. It must come on before 55 psi.

cards.q: How do you check that the spring brakes come on by themselves?
cards.a: Keep fanning off air. The parking brake valve pops out between 20 and 45 psi.

cards.q: How fast must a dual air system build pressure?
cards.a: From 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds at operating rpm.

cards.q: How do you test the parking brake?
cards.a: Put it on and pull gently against it in a low gear.

cards.q: At what speed do you test the service brakes?
cards.a: About five mph, applying the brakes firmly.

cards.q: What pressure is a fully charged air system?
cards.a: Typically 125 psi, with governor cutoff from 120 to 140 psi.

exam.q: With the brakes released, engine off, what is the most air a single vehicle may lose in one minute?
exam.why: Released: under 2 psi single, under 3 psi combination. Applied: 3 psi single, 4 psi combination.

exam.q: With the foot brake fully applied, what air loss in one minute is too much for a combination vehicle?
exam.why: Applied, a combination vehicle may not lose more than 4 psi in a minute.

exam.q: In a dual air system, pressure must build from 85 to 100 psi in how long?
exam.why: 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds at operating rpm.

reading.p: This is the air brake version of the step 7 brake check. Work through it in order.

Run the engine at a fast idle. The pumping should stop at about 125 psi and the gauge should stop rising. Then idle the engine and step on and off the brake to use air up. The pumping should start again at about 100 psi.
With the system fully charged, the engine off and the parking brake released, time the pressure drop for one minute.

numbers.what: in one minute, single vehicle
in one minute, combination vehicle

reading.p: Build the pressure to governor cutoff, shut the engine off, chock the wheels, release the parking brake and the tractor protection valve, then hold the foot brake down fully for one minute.

numbers.what: too much in one minute, single vehicle
too much in one minute, combination vehicle
the usual governor cutoff range, a full system being about 125 psi

reading.p: With enough pressure that the warning is off, shut the engine off, turn the electrical power on, and step on and off the brake pedal. The warning must come on before the pressure falls below 55 psi, in the tank with the lowest pressure on a dual system.

reading.h: 5. Spring brakes come on by themselves

reading.p: Keep using air up with the pedal. The parking brake valve should pop out, with the tractor protection valve on a tractor-trailer, between 20 and 45 psi. That puts the spring brakes on.

numbers.what: a dual air system, at operating rpm
a single air system made before 1975, idling at 600 to 900 rpm

ul: Parking brake: put it on and pull gently against it in a low gear, to check that it holds.
Service brakes: at normal pressure, with the parking brake off, roll forward at about five mph and apply the brakes firmly. Note any pull to one side, any odd feel, or a slow stop.

reading.note: If the governor, the warning or the leakage rate is wrong, do not drive. Have it fixed. You could lose the brakes on the road.

facts.text: For a normal stop, push the brake pedal down and control the pressure so the vehicle stops smoothly and safely.
With a manual transmission, do not push the clutch in until the engine rpm is down close to idle, and select a starting gear once you stop.

cards.q: When do you push the clutch in during a normal stop?
cards.a: Not until the engine rpm is down close to idle.

reading.p: Push the brake pedal down and control the pressure, so the vehicle comes to a smooth, safe stop.

reading.note: With a manual transmission, do not push the clutch in until the engine rpm is down close to idle. Once you stop, select a starting gear.

facts.text: Without ABS, hard braking on a slippery surface can lock the wheels. Locked steering wheels take away your steering, and other locked wheels can make you skid, jackknife or spin.
With ABS you brake as you always have: use only the braking force you need to stop safely and stay in control.
ABS on only the tractor, only the trailer, or only one axle still gives you more control, so brake normally.
If only the tractor has ABS, watch the trailer and let up on the brakes, if it is safe, should the trailer start to swing out.
If only the trailer has ABS, let up on the brakes, if it is safe, should you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife.
There is one exception: if you always drive with working ABS on every axle, you may fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop.
If your ABS fails you still have your normal brakes. Drive normally and get the system serviced soon.

cards.q: How do you brake in a tractor-trailer with ABS?
cards.a: The same as always: only the force you need to stop safely and stay in control.

cards.q: Only the trailer has ABS. What do you do if you start to jackknife?
cards.a: Let up on the brakes, if it is safe, until you have control.

cards.q: When may you fully apply the brakes in an emergency?
cards.a: Only if you always drive with working ABS on all axles.

cards.q: Your ABS light comes on. What brakes do you have?
cards.a: Your normal brakes. Drive normally and get it serviced soon.

exam.q: Your ABS malfunction lamp comes on while driving. What do you have?
exam.why: ABS is an addition. Without it you still have normal brakes, so drive normally and get it fixed.

reading.p: Brake hard on a slippery road without ABS and the wheels can lock. Locked steering wheels take your steering away. Other locked wheels can make you skid, jackknife or spin.

ABS senses a wheel about to lock, cuts the braking pressure to a safe level, and gives you back control. You may or may not stop faster, but you should be able to steer round an obstacle while braking.

ul: Brake as you always have.
Use only the braking force you need to stop safely and stay in control.
Brake the same way whether the ABS is on the tractor, the trailer or both.
As you slow, watch the tractor and trailer and ease off the brakes, if it is safe, to stay in control.

reading.h: When only one unit has ABS

ul: Only the tractor: you should keep steering control, and a jackknife is less likely. Watch the trailer and ease off the brakes if it starts to swing out.
Only the trailer: the trailer is less likely to swing out. If you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, ease off the brakes until you have control.

reading.note: One exception only: if you always drive a straight truck or a combination with working ABS on every axle, you may apply the brakes fully in an emergency stop.

reading.p: If the ABS fails you still have your normal brakes. Drive normally, and get the system serviced soon.

facts.text: In an emergency stop, brake so the vehicle stays in a straight line and you can still turn. Use controlled braking or stab braking.

Controlled braking: apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels, and keep steering movements very small. Release if a wheel locks or you must steer more, then re-apply as soon as you can.
Stab braking: apply the brakes all the way, release when the wheels lock, and apply fully again as soon as the wheels start rolling.
It can take up to one second for the wheels to start rolling after you release the brakes, and re-applying too early stops the vehicle straightening out.

cards.q: What are the two emergency braking methods?
cards.a: Controlled braking and stab braking.

cards.q: Describe controlled braking.
cards.a: Brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels, with very small steering movements.

cards.q: Describe stab braking.
cards.a: Full brakes, release when the wheels lock, full brakes again once they roll.

cards.q: How long can it take for wheels to roll again after releasing the brakes?
cards.a: Up to one second.

exam.q: In stab braking, when do you release the brakes?
exam.why: Apply fully, release when the wheels lock, then apply fully again when they start rolling.

reading.p: If someone pulls out in front of you, braking is the right answer when you have room to stop and you brake properly. Brake so the vehicle stays in a straight line and you can still turn. There are two methods.

ul: Apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels.
Keep steering movements very small.
If a wheel locks, or you must steer more, release the brakes and re-apply as soon as you can.
Apply the brakes all the way.
Release them when the wheels lock.
Apply fully again as soon as the wheels start rolling.

reading.note: It can take up to one second for the wheels to roll again after you release. Re-apply too early and the vehicle will not straighten out.

facts.text: Brake lag is the time the brakes need to work after you push the pedal, and with air brakes it is half a second or more.
Total stopping distance with air brakes has four parts: perception distance, reaction distance, brake lag distance, and braking distance.
Air brake lag adds about 32 feet at 55 mph on dry pavement.
At 55 mph, for an average driver with good traction and brakes, total stopping distance is over 450 feet.

cards.q: What is brake lag?
cards.a: The time air brakes need to work after you push the pedal: half a second or more.

cards.q: What are the four parts of air brake stopping distance?
cards.a: Perception, reaction, brake lag and braking distance.

cards.q: How much does brake lag add at 55 mph?
cards.a: About 32 feet.

cards.q: What is total stopping distance at 55 mph with air brakes?
cards.a: Over 450 feet.

exam.q: Which distance do air brakes add that hydraulic brakes do not?
exam.why: Air takes time to reach the brakes, so brake lag distance is added: about 32 feet at 55 mph.

exam.q: Total stopping distance at 55 mph with air brakes is about:
exam.why: Perception, reaction, brake lag and braking add to over 450 feet at 55 mph.

reading.p: Air brakes add a delay that hydraulic brakes do not have. Hydraulic brakes work at once. With air brakes it takes half a second or more for the air to travel down the lines to the brakes. That delay is brake lag.
Perception distance, plus reaction distance, plus brake lag distance, plus braking distance, is your total stopping distance.

numbers.what: what brake lag adds at 55 mph on dry pavement
total stopping distance at 55 mph, average driver, good brakes and traction

facts.text: Brakes fade or fail from too much heat, caused by using them too much instead of using the braking effect of the engine.
Heat changes the brake lining chemically, which cuts friction, and it expands the drums, so the shoes must move farther and press with less force.
Brakes out of adjustment stop doing their share first, so the others overheat and fade. Check brake adjustment often, because brakes go out of adjustment quickly when hot.

cards.q: What causes brake fade?
cards.a: Too much heat from overusing the brakes instead of the engine's braking effect.

cards.q: How does heat cause fade?
cards.a: It changes the lining chemically and expands the drums, so contact force drops.

reading.p: Brakes slow the vehicle by rubbing, and rubbing makes heat. Brakes are built to take a lot of heat, but they can fade or fail when they get too hot. That comes from using the brakes too much instead of using the braking effect of the engine.

ul: It changes the brake lining chemically, which cuts the friction.
It expands the drums, so the shoes must move farther to touch them, and they press with less force.

reading.p: Keep going and the fade grows until the vehicle will not slow down.

reading.note: Adjustment matters too. A brake out of adjustment stops doing its share first, so the others overheat and fade. Brakes go out of adjustment quickly when hot, so check the adjustment often.

facts.text: On a long or steep downgrade, the brakes are only a help to the braking effect of the engine, so get into the proper low gear first.

Proper downgrade braking: apply the brakes just hard enough to feel a definite slowdown, then release when your speed is about five mph below your safe speed, and the application should last about three seconds.
Apply the brakes again once the speed comes back up to your safe speed, and repeat to the bottom of the grade.

cards.q: On a steep downgrade, what slows the vehicle most?
cards.a: The engine. The brakes only help it, so be in the proper low gear.

cards.q: Describe proper downgrade braking.
cards.a: Brake to a definite slowdown, release about five mph below your safe speed, about three seconds per application.

cards.q: Your safe speed is 40 mph. How do you brake on the grade?
cards.a: Brake at 40, slow to 35, release, and repeat as needed.

exam.q: Your safe speed on a downgrade is 40 mph. When do you release the brakes?
exam.why: Brake at your safe speed and release about five mph below it, so 40 down to 35.

exam.q: How long should each brake application last on a downgrade?
exam.why: The application should last about three seconds, and take off about five mph.

reading.p: On a long or steep downgrade the brakes only help the engine. The engine does the work, so get into the proper low gear before you start down.

ul: Apply the brakes just hard enough to feel a definite slowdown.
When your speed is about five mph below your safe speed, release the brakes. The application should last about three seconds.
When the speed comes back up to your safe speed, do it again.

reading.p: For a safe speed of 40 mph: do not brake until you reach 40, brake down to 35, release, and repeat to the bottom of the grade.

facts.text: If the low air pressure warning comes on, stop and park safely as soon as you can, because there may be an air leak.
Controlled braking works only while enough air is left in the tanks, and the spring brakes come on between 20 and 45 psi.
A heavily loaded vehicle takes a long way to stop on spring brakes, because the spring brakes do not work on every axle.
A lightly loaded vehicle, or one on a slippery road, may skid out of control when the spring brakes come on.

cards.q: Why stop early when the low air warning comes on?
cards.a: Controlled braking only works while air remains, and spring brakes come on at 20 to 45 psi.

cards.q: Why is stopping on spring brakes dangerous when heavily loaded?
cards.a: Spring brakes do not work on all axles, so it takes a long distance.

reading.p: If the low air pressure warning comes on, stop and park safely as soon as you can. There may be a leak in the system.

ul: Controlled braking works only while enough air is left in the tanks.
The spring brakes come on between 20 and 45 psi.
A heavily loaded vehicle needs a long way to stop on spring brakes, because they do not work on every axle.
A lightly loaded vehicle, or one on a slippery road, may skid out of control when the spring brakes come on.

reading.note: It is much safer to stop while you still have air for the foot brakes.

facts.text: Use the parking brakes any time you park, except when the brakes are very hot or very wet in freezing weather.
Very hot brakes can be damaged by the heat if you set the parking brake, so let them cool and use wheel chocks on level ground.
Very wet brakes in freezing weather can freeze on, so drive in a low gear with light brake pressure to heat and dry them.
Drain the air tanks at the end of each working day unless the vehicle has automatic drains, or the brakes could fail.
Never leave your vehicle unattended without the parking brakes on or the wheels chocked.

cards.q: When do you NOT use the parking brakes?
cards.a: When the brakes are very hot, or very wet in freezing weather.

cards.q: What do you do with very hot brakes at a stop?
cards.a: Let them cool, and hold the vehicle with wheel chocks on level ground.

cards.q: How do you dry wet brakes?
cards.a: Drive in a low gear and use the brakes lightly to heat and dry them.

cards.q: May you leave the vehicle briefly without the parking brake?
cards.a: No. Never leave it unattended without parking brakes on or wheels chocked.

exam.q: You have just come down a steep grade and the brakes are very hot. What do you do when you park?
choices: Set the parking brakes at once
Let the brakes cool and use wheel chocks
Set the parking brakes and the trailer brakes
exam.why: Very hot brakes can be damaged by the heat, so let them cool and chock the wheels on level ground.

exam.q: You will be away from the vehicle for two minutes. What must you do?
choices: Apply the parking brakes or chock the wheels
exam.why: Never leave a vehicle unattended without the parking brakes applied or the wheels chocked.

reading.p: Use the parking brakes any time you park. Pull the control knob out to apply them and push it in to release. On a newer vehicle it is a yellow, diamond-shaped knob marked parking brakes. On an older one it may be a round blue knob, another shape, or a lever.

reading.h: Two times not to use them

ul: Very hot brakes, just off a steep grade: the heat can damage them. Let them cool, and hold the vehicle with wheel chocks on level ground.
Very wet brakes in freezing weather: they can freeze on, and the vehicle cannot move. Drive in a low gear and brake lightly to heat and dry them.

reading.note: Never leave your vehicle unattended without the parking brakes on or the wheels chocked. It could roll away and hurt somebody.

reading.p: If the vehicle has no automatic tank drains, drain the air tanks at the end of each working day, to get the water and oil out. If you do not, the brakes could fail.
